segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: You are now 20 minutes early, which gives Connor time to reconsider the plan entirely.

segments.speaker: Connor
segments.text: Do you think we should try-- I know you plan on doing the note, but do you think that we should call him?

segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: Yeah, but we already tried calling.

segments.speaker: Connor
segments.text: But we call his barbershop and be like, hey, I've got an appointment for him at 5 o'clock. He'll say, yeah, sure, let me check.

segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: And then what, say exactly what's in the note? Say we're outside?

segments.speaker: Connor
segments.text: Hey, yeah, this is your sons.

segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: What if he hangs up?

segments.speaker: Connor
segments.text: Then we go in there.

segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: And do what?

segments.speaker: Connor
segments.text: We say, fuck you.

segments.speaker: Connor
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Connor
segments.text: I don't know. I'm OK with doing that. I've always wanted to say fuck you to dad. Do you want to go in together? Would that make you feel better about it?

segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: I mean, if you want to, I'm down.

segments.speaker: Connor
segments.text: I want him to look at us in the case that he decides that he doesn't want to deal with it, so that he can at least do it once if he decides to avoid conversation with us, at least going in there and him seeing our face. I can be like, hey, I'm here, and I see you.

segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: OK, two minutes. One minute till 5:00. OK. Are you ready?

segments.speaker: Connor
segments.text: Yeah, you?

segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: As ready as I can be.

segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: [CHATTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The first words your birth father ever says to you-- do you have an appointment?

segments.speaker: Sayre Quevedo
segments.text: Yeah, 5:00.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You sit down and wait your turn. You can barely get yourself to look up at him. You fix your eyes first on the wine-colored tiles, then the client's sneakers slack against the footrest, the shapeless, oversized black barber's tarp, then your father's hands as he trims stray hairs, chatting easily over the jazz music playing softly over the speakers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The walls are lined with framed photographs of what you assume were once famous Hollywood actors whose faces you do not recognize and names you do not know. In the corner, a magazine rack full of vintage Playboy magazines. Your birth father brushes clean his client's forehead and nape with a blond duster brush, says goodbye cheerily. He glances over at you and Connor and then calmly walks to the back door of the shop. He disappears for five seconds, then 10, then 15. He returns with a broom and slowly, methodically sweeps the hair into a dustbin and then the trash.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You imagine everything leading up to this moment from his point of view. Today he woke up, probably had a coffee, kissed his wife goodbye, drove to work, attended to some regulars, made small talk about the relief of 70-degree weather or the impending invasion of Ukraine as he lined up their beards and hairlines-- took a quick lunch break, scrolled on Facebook on his phone. Ten minutes ago, he probably looked up at the clock, saw two young guys walk in, and felt a wave of relief, the last customers. As he finished sweeping the hair into a bin, he was probably hit with the feeling of relaxation that comes with knowing that the day is nearly done.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now he calls those boys up to the chair. One of them, the curly-haired one who can barely look him in the eye, pulls a note from his pocket and hands it to him. His name is written on the front, and both boys walk out wordlessly. And now, what has been up until this moment a very ordinary day, has become a monumental one in just a few seconds.
